name: Undercut / fade with textured top

card.summary: A short-sided haircut with longer styled top, widely recommended for many face shapes; popularity is documented, attractiveness effects unstudied.
card.note: Claims of suiting many face shapes come from stylists and forums, not studies.

lead: The undercut is a hairstyle in which the sides and back are shaved or clipped very short while the top is left long, often parted and styled. A fade tapers the sides gradually, and a textured top refers to the longer hair styled with product for volume or a matte finish.[1][2]

Wikipedia traces the undercut to early 20th-century working-class men, mainstream popularity in the 1920s and 1930s, and a revival in the early 2010s, with adopters including David Beckham.[1] It is frequently cited in men's grooming advice as a default flattering cut; no studies were found testing that claim.

paras: The undercut shaves the sides along a line above the ears with a longer top. The fade is a taper from short to longer, set by clipper guard size.[1][2]

The cut was associated in the early 1900s with working-class youth and gangs such as Glasgow's Neds, Manchester's Scuttlers and Birmingham's Peaky Blinders, was common in the Jazz Age and 1940s, and faded in the 1960s as longer styles took over. It returned in the late 1980s among new wave fans, and in the 2010s among hipsters and others; by 2014 it was relatively mainstream in the UK.[1] In the late 2010s some press linked it to alt-right figures, and some critics described a resemblance to historical styles.[1]

Forums and stylists often recommend contrast between short sides and textured top to add height or draw attention away from the jaw or forehead. Specific recommendations by face shape are opinion-based.

timeline.event: Undercut mainstream in the Jazz Age.[1]
Revival among hipsters, skaters and celebrities.[1]

lore.intro: The undercut or fade with textured top is a frequent "safe default" recommendation in grooming communities.

claims.claim: This cut flatters many face shapes.
claims.believers: Proponents say contrast between sides and top adds height and structure.
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing face-shape suitability; Wikipedia documents history and popularity only.[1]

claims.claim: Skin fades make the face and jaw look sharper.
claims.believers: Users say short sides emphasize the jawline.
claims.experts: No research was found on perceived attractiveness of fades.
